summary: One of the periodic IAB status reports on which Internet protocols were at which stage of standardization. It gives an overview of the standards procedures and the RFC series, explains the terms used, and lists protocols. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1100.

eli5.summary: A school keeps a chart saying which lessons are finished and which are still being worked on. This is the chart for Internet rules, and it was updated again later.

subtitle: The Internet standards status report from December 1988: which protocols were standard, draft, proposed, experimental or historic.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed a single, authoritative, regularly updated list stating which protocols had official status, which were still in development, and which had been superseded or abandoned.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB published a quarterly memo explaining the standardization process, describing the RFC series, defining standard/draft/proposed/experimental/historic states and required/recommended/elective/not-recommended statuses, then listing all known Internet protocols in a matrix of their current categorization.
tldr.outcome: This snapshot from December 1988 shows TCP, UDP, SMTP, FTP and the Domain Name System as recommended standards, while protocols like SGMP (later replaced by SNMP) were already historic. The document was replaced by RFC 1100, then became the basis for the periodic Internet Standards documents still published today.

facts.label: Recommended standard protocols in 1988
facts.value: UDP, TCP, DNS, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, Mail, EGP

today: RFC 1083 is marked historic and was replaced by RFC 1100, which is itself now historic. The concept of the quarterly IAB standards list continued and evolved into the modern STD (Internet Standard) numbers and the periodic official standards lists. Today the IETF maintains the current standards status through the RFC editor and IETF consensus processes.

sections.title: The Standardization Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1083 explains how the Internet Activities Board (IAB) managed protocol standardization. Protocols could be proposed by anyone in the Internet community by writing and submitting an RFC. The IAB assigned proposed protocols to working groups for review and development, and the recommendation of the working group received major consideration in the IAB's decision to assign a state and status to the protocol.

The general policy was not to designate a protocol as an official standard until there was implementation experience with it. The IAB reserved the use of the term standard in any RFC to only those protocols which the IAB had formally approved, though some vendor protocols became important without IAB approval.
sections.eli5: Anyone can suggest a new rule, but it has to be tested and improved before the school officially adopts it.

sections.title: States and Statuses
sections.content:
RFC 1083 defines two independent categorizations for each protocol. The state describes its place in the standardization process: standard (officially approved), draft standard (under community review), proposed (in development with implementation), experimental (research or special-purpose), or historic (superseded or abandoned).

The status indicates implementation expectation: required (all systems must implement), recommended (systems should implement), elective (optional, implement if functionality is needed), or not recommended (use discouraged, typical for experimental or historic protocols).
sections.eli5: State is whether the rule is being worked on or is done. Status is whether everyone needs to follow it, everyone should, or it is optional.

sections.title: The Development Path
sections.content:
A new protocol typically started in the proposed or experimental state as elective or not recommended. After implementation and testing, it could advance to draft standard with recommended status. Once draft standard had been reviewed by the entire community for typically six months without serious objections, the IAB could declare it an official standard.

Protocols that became superseded by better designs or fell unused were designated historic. Few protocols were required of all systems because of the variety of possible system types: gateways need not implement TCP (though useful), while general-purpose hosts should implement IP including ICMP, TCP, UDP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, Mail and DNS.
sections.eli5: New ideas start simple and optional. If everyone likes them, they move up. If they get replaced by better ideas, they are marked as old.

sections.title: The December 1988 Standards List
sections.content:
RFC 1083 lists the protocols under each categorization. Standard protocols included IP and its amendments (subnetting, broadcast datagrams), ICMP, UDP, TCP, the Domain Name System, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, mail message format and EGP. NetBIOS, Echo, Discard, Character Generator, Quote of the Day, Active Users and Time Server were elective.

Draft standard protocols included SNMP, the Management Information Base, the Structure of Management Information, the Network Time Protocol, the Internet Group Multicast Protocol and Bootstrap Protocol. Proposed protocols ranged from Remote Procedure Call to Finger to Trivial File Transfer. Experimental protocols included IP MTU discovery and the Interactive Mail Access Protocol. Historic protocols like the Simple Gateway Monitoring Protocol (SGMP) had been replaced by newer standards.
sections.eli5: TCP and UDP were done, SNMP was almost done, RPC and Finger were being worked on, and SGMP was old and replaced.
